Thanks for the feedback.

I am not sure though if guanidine carbonate is the same as mixing TMG with sodium carbonate.

In his Applied Optics paper Jeff explicitly mentions guanidine carbonate: “...the TMG was substituted with guanidine (as carbonate salt). This worked surprisingly well at enabling holograms to be produced at exposure levels between two and three times longer than those used with TMG in the formulation. This put guanidine in the same class of effectiveness as tri-n-propylamine but without the malodorous nature of the letter.”

My hope would have been that guanidine carbonate produces layers that are less hygroscopic than the ones made with TMG. Since guanidine carbonate is widely used for cosmetics I would have expected that it's easier to find than TMG. Furthermore, it may be used without adding any acid. So adjusting the pH value may no longer be necessary.

Hi Ahmet, As I see it you ideally need to have the TMG or plain quanidine, free and unattached to an acid, but it can be too strong a base and can hydrolyse the gelatin. So you can rein it back a bit with a weak acid so that there is still free base there in equilibrium. Tetramethyl quanidine or plain Quanidine salts of strong acids (nitrates, chlorides, sulfates) are not likely to be of any use because there is in them no significant free base available.

Jeff

I would not worry much about photobleaching (without chromate) at this point. The speed that you describe is about the same as what I experienced when doing the same experiment a year ago.

A good test to see if you get a reaction is to cover half of the plate and then expose. If you then wash the plate afterwards you should see a clear ridge at the border where the cover was. If you don't see the ridge, don't worry. Perhaps the water was too cold. After you have washed out all the blue MB coloring with cold water, put the plate in a bath of say 25 degrees C and see if you now get the differential swelling between covered and uncovered area's.

posts.content_md:
> All plates were transparent and slightly blue before exposure. Some plates had a very uniform matted glass like look after processing.

After you took off the cover plate and after drying, but BEFORE exposure, did your plates look less blue than when the cover plate was still on. This would be a big clue. If the plates loose transparency during drying that means that the MB did not stay dissolved. This usually happens if the environment where one dries the plate is very humid. In that case the plate looses nearly all sensitivity.

I think there can only be one of two things happening with your plates:

- The plates were dried too long and most of the TMG was lost from the gelatin. **OR**

- The plates were dried in a too humid environment and the MB did not stay dissolved. This can be easily seen if the plate looses much of it's blue colour.

I have had trouble with this too in the past (now my lab is moisture controlled). I found that it can be solved by drying the plates in a box that also has a sponge in it that has been soaked with some 25% TMG solution. This solution does two things: There remains more TMG in the plates + the MB is less likely to get out of solution because there is less loss of TMG.

Yes, I agree with Jeff. If there is a variation in thickness you will see it instantly. Even very small variations in intensity of the laser with respect to location on the plate (dust on the lens) will show up clearly as soon as you let the water drip off the plate. If you don't clearly see any variations in thickness then they are simply not there.

Yesterday I tested one of my new MBDCG plates. This time 10% (of the weight of gelatine) glycerine was added. The plate was 24hrs old.

The plate was first processed at a water temperature of 26C. It remained uniformly transparent during all baths and after drying.

Reprocessed at 28C the plate turned slightly milky but was clear after drying. During drying the lettering was visible for a couple of seconds, then disappeared.

At 31C the plate turned milkier and was slightly milky after drying. No lettering visible.

The plate was stripewise exposed, but i'm not sure if it was the region with 50-150mj/cm2 or 250-650mJ/cm2 in which the letters temporarily showed up.

Today I tested the now 2 days old plates with 100/200/300/400/500mJ and with water temperatures of 24-33C. No relief image. No signs of any kind of photo reaction. 

Just like yesterday, the plates either remained transparent or got different grades of milkiness depending on the temperature.

Not sure what to try next.

The DCG formulas we post here are strictly a phase material. When the processing there should be no image at all unless it is being recreated in phase. What that means is the exposed areas only have a different index of refraction than the non-exposed areas. I would not expect to see a transparency exposed without interference unless it was a surface releif while the gelatine was exposed and in its most swelled state.
